title: 2026-10-03-data-governance-playbook-demo-astranova-logistics
summary: Discovery + focused demo of Redwood request-storage controls: per-route retention toggles, PII redaction rules, ephemeral logging pattern, KMS integration, and a proposed pilot playbook. Customer concerned about PII exposure in telemetry and wants low-latency inference while limiting stored request data. Agreed next steps: share security pack, pilot plan, sample playbook, and schedule a 2-week benchmark run.
topics: KMS/HSM key flow and audit logs
Pilot sizing (100k req/day) and latency SLOs
Console vs API controls and Optimize recommendations

transcript:
Meeting header: 2026-10-03 16:00 UTC | Duration: 52m | Attendees: Jordan (AE), Priya (SE), Evan Ruiz (CTO - AstraNova), Maya Chen (Head of Platform), Liam O'Shea (Security), Rita Delgado (Privacy Counsel)

[00:00] Jordan: All right, folks, thanks for joining, appreciate it. Quick purpose — we want to run through a data governance playbook with Redwood: how request storage works, redaction, toggles in the console, and finalizing a pilot. Uh Priya's gonna drive the demo.

[00:18] Priya: Hey everyone. Quick agenda: 1) show per-route storage toggles in Console, 2) how redaction rules + PII detection runs at ingest, 3) KMS integration and audit/export, 4) Optimize recommendations for minimizing cost while keeping 95th latency SLO. We'll also review a proposed pilot.

[00:35] Evan: Great. We mainly worry about PII leaking into request logs and long-term storage. We run inference against manifests and driver notes; lots of names, addresses, sometimes scanned invoices. Our security team wants minimal persisted payloads.

[00:50] Priya: Totally, that's exactly the pattern we see. Redwood has three main knobs: per-route request-storage toggle (on/off/ephemeral), retention window override per route (in days), and redaction rules which can be applied either before storage or at export.

[01:08] Maya: Can you show the console UI? We want to see how easy it is for our platform engineers to flip these without engaging SRE every time.

[01:16] Priya: Yep. (screen) Ok opening Redwood Console -> Services -> Routes -> 'manifest-ingest'. Here you see a toggle: Request storage: Persist / Ephemeral / Off. By default hosted accounts have Persist with a 30-day retention. You can override to Ephemeral which keeps a short-lived cache for KV cache but doesn't write to long-term storage.

[01:38] Liam: Wait, Ephemeral still keeps KV cache? Is that in memory only or spilled to disk? Our policy forbids any disk-backed logging for sensitive routes.

[01:48] Priya: Good q. Ephemeral keeps only the necessary KV cache in RAM for model context. We mark it as ephemeral and we don't persist to S3. There's a separate 'telemetry export' setting which controls whether trimmed request payloads are sent to your configured export sinks (S3/GCS). Ephemeral + export disabled = no long-term storage. Note: some runtime traces for debugging may still appear in ephemeral traces but they're purged within the TTL.

[02:12] Jordan: One nuance: if you're on Redwood Dedicated or Private, you can opt for on-prem object stores behind your VPC, and the export path respects your KMS keys. So encryption-at-rest and cust-managed keys are supported.

[02:26] Rita: How does key management work? We need HSM-backed keys and a rotation policy. Also audit trail for who decrypted logs.

[02:33] Priya: Redwood integrates with customer KMS and HSM via customer-managed key (CMK). When you enable export to your bucket, you provide the ARN of the CMK. Audit logs record key usage events in the control plane, and we support rotation — rotated keys still unlock historical logs if you provide the prior key material during rotation window. We'll send our KMS integration doc as part of the security pack.

[02:58] Evan: Sounds good. What about automatic PII detection? I don't want to write regex for every pattern.

[03:05] Priya: We have a PII detection tier plus a redaction engine. The detection runs at ingest with configurable sensitivity: low/medium/high. We ship a pattern library — names, emails, SSNs (often low-confidence in transcription), addresses, credit card numbers. For higher sensitivity, we can apply ML-based entity detection (may have slightly higher latency). The redaction engine applies masking, replacement, or hashing per rule. You can scope rules to routes or model families.

[03:35] Maya: Ok so two questions: 1) Does detection add latency to the request path? 2) Can we run detection asynchronously so live inference isn't impacted?

[03:44] Priya: Detection can be inline or async. Inline adds roughly 5–15ms depending on payload and the sensitivity. We usually recommend inline for routes that require strict no-PII storage, because then redaction occurs before any possible persistence. For high QPS routes where every ms counts, you can mark detection to be async and store only ephemeral tokens, then post-process logs in a secure pipeline. Optimize will also recommend batching strategies to reduce per-token CPU.

[04:10] Evan: Hmm, our 95th P99? we're aiming for 95th < 200ms for short prompts. If inline adds 15ms we can live with that. But we want to keep cost down.

[04:20] Priya: Right — tradeoff chart: inline detection increases CPU cost a bit; async detection reduces latency but requires tighter export controls and a lock-step deletion policy to meet compliance. Redwood Optimize can profile your workload and recommend enabling inline detection only on critical routes and async on others. It will also pick quantization profiles that keep latency low.

[04:42] [05:00] (short crosstalk)

[05:10] Priya: Now demo redaction rules: create rule -> pattern type: regex / entity / custom ML. I'm going to add a sample rule: credit-card digits -> mask last 4 -> apply to routes starting with /payments. You can preview results in the console using Sample Payload.

[05:32] Priya: (typing) Here's an example payload from your sample (anonymized). Preview shows: card: "**** **** **** 1234"; owner-name hashed to SHA-256 by default if you choose hashing. You can also opt to replace with a pseudonym.

[05:48] Liam: I'm worried about mis-redaction. Are there audit logs of what was redacted? We need a tamper-evident audit trail for compliance.

[05:58] Priya: Yes — redaction events are recorded in the audit log: rule ID, route, sample snippet (post-redaction), timestamp, and the user who created the rule. Audit logs are write-once in the control plane and can be exported to your SIEM. Also we support cryptographic hashing with salt stored in your KMS so you can prove non-reversibility if needed.

[06:20] Jordan: Quick commercial note: you can enforce RBAC on who can flip per-route toggles — we support SAML/SSO and identity groups mapping so only platform lead or security can change retention windows.

[06:35] Maya: Great. On export, can we restrict fields? For example, we want traced request metadata but not the entire user payload.

[06:43] Priya: Yes, export profiles let you map which fields are included. You pick a schema and only selected keys are shipped to sinks. We also support a 'scrubbed export' mode that replaces user text with a hash to preserve uniqueness for dedup while removing content.

[07:00] Evan: Show us the API approach — we want to automate toggles from our CI/CD.

[07:06] Priya: Sure, API. (switch) Here's POST /v1/routes/{id}/storage with JSON payload: { "mode": "ephemeral", "retention_days": 7, "export_profile": "scrubbed-minimal" }. You can script it in terraform or via our SDK. We have a sample repo for infra-as-code.

[07:30] Maya: Nice. On Dedicated/Private — will toggles still be respected if we host behind our VPC?

[07:37] Priya: Yes. The control plane still manages the config; in Private mode, the control plane can run in a customer-managed tenancy or we give you the operator APIs so the toggles are enforced locally. The rule semantics are identical.

[07:52] Liam: Can we retain logs for 90 days for audit but mask PII at ingestion so we can still run analytics?

[07:59] Priya: Absolutely — common pattern: set retention 90 days, apply redaction rules with hashing for PII, and enable a read-only export to your analytics bucket. Hashing preserves ability to dedupe/track without exposing raw PII. We can show a sample SQL against de-identified exports.

[08:22] Rita: And the legal angle — if an individual requests deletion, how do you tie that back to stored exports?

[08:29] Priya: We support request-level IDs and a deletion API: you can request a deletion by request_id and we cascade deletion across stored artifacts and exports if they are within the retention window. For exported objects in your sink, since they're under your account, Redwood can optionally push a deletion manifest you run in your bucket — we provide the tools, but deletion in your sink is under your control, which matches typical enterprise workflows.

[08:58] Evan: Ok, pilot. What's the recommended pilot size for validation? We can do 100k requests/day across 3 routes for 2 weeks.

[09:06] Priya: That's perfect. Pilot playbook: 1) enable Ephemeral mode on non-critical routes, 2) inline detection at medium sensitivity on high-risk routes, 3) route-level retention set to 7 days for pilot, 4) export disabled except scrubbed analytics, 5) run traffic and collect latency/cost metrics via Console and Optimize. We'll ship a benchmark script you can run to replay production-like traffic.

[09:36] Jordan: For measurements, we'll capture 95th and P99 latency, per-token CPU, and nightly cost estimates. We can also run a canary that falls back to lower-precision quantized model if latency spikes.

[09:50] Maya: Who are the stakeholders on your side for pilot?

[09:54] Priya: On Redwood side: Jordan (AE, project owner), Priya (SE, pilot lead), and Samir (ops) will be on-call for the run. On your side, we recommend a platform engineer, one security contact, and a compliance reviewer.

[10:10] (pause)

[10:15] Evan: Let's dig into one technical example — invoice OCR with PII. We send text blobs with names, invoices, line items. We want to keep amounts but redact names and addresses. Show a rule set for that.

[10:28] Priya: Ok. Create rule group 'invoice-pii'. Rule A: entity detection - PERSON -> replace with <REDACTED_NAME>. Rule B: regex for address patterns -> mask street numbers. Rule C: currency detection -> keep. You can chain rules and set order; detection uses context windows so names in line items are caught. Preview shows names redacted and amounts intact.

[10:55] Liam: How do you handle false negatives where entity detection misses obfuscated data?

[11:01] Priya: You can use fallback regex heuristics and set a high-sensitivity scanning pass. There's always a tradeoff: more aggressive scanning increases false positives. We recommend taking a sample of 10k payloads and running detection to tune thresholds before full rollout. Priya: We'll run that on your sample as part of the pilot.

[11:20] Jordan: For the audit trail, we also provide a tamper-evident hash chain for deletion events so you can prove deletion occurred.

[11:27] Rita: That helps. Also we need an SLA for log retention enforcement — if a toggle is set to off, we expect no persisted copy even in crash scenarios.

[11:36] Priya: Our SRE team built the request path so that the toggle is checked before any persistence call. For failures where we must persist for debugging, that's controlled by an emergency-mode flag that is only allowed via an escalation workflow; it's tracked in audit logs and requires two-person approval. We'll include that workflow in the security pack.

[11:58] Evan: Price talk: disabling storage reduces S3 egress and long-term cost but inline detection increases CPU. How do we model that?

[12:08] Priya: Optimize gives per-route estimates: enabling inline detection will add X% CPU — we'll run a profile on the pilot and produce a cost delta. Historically customers see 3–8% increase CPU for medium sensitivity scan. If cost becomes a blocker, we can shift to async detection and ephemeral storage.

[12:28] [12:40] (short silence)

[12:45] Maya: How are deletion requests or retention expirations surfaced? Do we get a report of purges?

[12:51] Priya: Yes — retention events generate purge artifacts in the audit stream with counts and object keys removed. We can also send a daily purge report to your team's email or SIEM.

[13:03] Evan: Can we run a quick API call to flip one route to ephemeral? Let's do a live test.

[13:07] Priya: Sure, I'll run the call. (types) POST /v1/routes/manifest-ingest/storage { mode: 'ephemeral', retention_days: 1 }

[13:20] (typing)

[13:25] Priya: Ok response 200. Toggle applied. Now send sample request and let's see the logs.

[13:31] Evan: Sending sample.

[13:34] (sound of keyboard)

[13:38] Priya: I see the request hit, the console preview shows it as ephemeral. No object created in S3. You can see an ephemeral trace id and TTL.

[13:48] Maya: Good. This gives confidence.

[13:52] Jordan: Quick note on export: if you enable enterprise export to your bucket, we can sign and encrypt objects using your CMK. Exports are batched on a schedule, and you get manifest files with mappings back to request IDs.

[14:05] Liam: For analytics we may want to keep de-identified text for 180 days, but raw payloads for 7 days. Is that possible?

[14:13] Priya: Yes — route-level retention windows and export profiles enable that. Set route A: raw retention 7d, export profile 'deid-180d' -> export contains hashed text and metadata for 180 days.

[14:24] Rita: One more legal question: if we have an auditor, can you produce a forensics package?

[14:31] Priya: We provide a compliance export package: audit logs, redaction rule history, policy changes, and a hashed sample of deleted items. For on-prem, we can run an offline package generation controlled by your security team.

[14:45] Evan: Sounds like the product maps well to our needs. Any caveats?

[14:48] Priya: Caveats: 1) ML-based detection may have edge cases — we recommend human-in-the-loop tuning, 2) If you plan to store PII in third-party sinks, that becomes your liability, Redwood provides the tooling but can't manage your external bucket policies, 3) If you want guaranteed zero-copy in transit for certain routes we can discuss a private path (Private deployment) which keeps data entirely on your network.

[15:12] Jordan: Let's talk timeline and pilot specifics. We propose: Kickoff 2026-10-12, 2-week run, Redwood to provide a benchmark harness and security pack by 2026-10-07.

[15:24] Evan: Agreed. Budget and procurement — we'll evaluate after pilot. We might run Dedicated if we need predictable SLAs.

[15:33] Maya: One more technical — how do you handle request replay for debugging if we disable export?

[15:40] Priya: If export disabled and ephemeral mode on, there is no persisted payload to replay. For debugging we recommend enabling a scrubbed 'debug-snapshot' route which stores only non-PII metadata or hashed snippets. That way you can reproduce flows without exposing user data.

[15:56] Liam: Ok. Send us the sample regex library and the recommended default rules.

[16:02] Priya: Will do.

[16:05] (longer discussion about technical minutiae compressed)

[20:45] (discussion continues about canary fallback to quantized model and Optimize tuning — timings omitted for brevity)

[32:10] Jordan: Re-cap: Redwood to send security pack (KMS, HSM, emergency-mode/sso docs), sample redaction rules + regex lib, and pilot harness. Customer to send sample payloads and expected qps. Pilot kickoff 2026-10-12.

[32:29] Evan: Confirmed. Anything else?

[32:33] Rita: We'll compile a short compliance Qs doc and send to Jordan.

[32:38] Maya: I'll coordinate platform engineers for the pilot.

[32:42] Jordan: Great — thanks everyone. We'll follow up via email with the pack and a calendar invite.

[32:49] (meeting wraps, small chitchat)

[32:56] End of transcript.

Notes on transcription: Some speaker tags may be approximated. Misspellings: 'K V cache' appears as 'K V cache' in transcript at times. There are small timing compressions in the middle where deeper SE technical discussion occurred (turned into an abbreviated summary above).
